descriptors.title: Digital systems and components
descriptors.description: identify and explore digital systems and their components for a purpose
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise and explore digital systems (hardware and software) for a purpose (AC9TDIFK01). They have identified some hardware and software components used for familiar purposes. They have not yet identified components by name or explained how component combinations enable a system's purpose.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify digital systems in familiar contexts and explain how components (input, output, storage, processing) work together to serve a purpose.

nodes.label: What digital systems are
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify familiar digital systems (devices) in their home and school environment and name what they are used for
criteria: Names at least two different digital systems correctly
States a distinct purpose for each system

width.minimum: Name at least two different digital systems encountered at home or school and state a purpose for each
width.typical: Identify multiple digital systems (tablet, computer, TV, interactive display, camera) in familiar settings; explain how each is used at home or school
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians in remote communities access and use digital systems for essential services — identifying specific systems and the communities they serve
Compare digital systems used at school with those used at home — identify which system is used for each purpose and why they may differ

modes.reason: Students often conflate the term 'computer' with all digital systems, missing that a TV remote, tablet, and interactive whiteboard are all distinct digital systems. Encountering a range of contexts (home, school, community) helps students build a reliable category for 'digital system' rather than a narrow exemplar.

nodes.label: Components of digital systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and name components of digital systems — including input devices, output devices and storage
criteria: Correctly names at least one input and one output component on a digital system
Explains what each named component does in plain language
nodes.hinge_reason: Component categorisation errors (swapping input/output) propagate directly into Node 3 — students who cannot reliably identify and categorise components cannot explain how they coordinate to serve a purpose.

width.minimum: Identify and name at least one input and one output component on a familiar digital system; explain what each component does
width.typical: Identify input devices (keyboard, touchpad, camera, microphone), output devices (screen, speakers, printer) and storage on common digital systems; explain the function of each component type
wider: Explore how the same component serves different purposes on different devices — for example how a screen is both output on a laptop and also input (touch) on a tablet
Investigate a camera on a device: identify it as an input component and explain how it enables different purposes (photos, video calls, scanning)

modes.reason: Component naming requires accurate recall and correct categorisation (input/output/storage). Students commonly swap input and output. Practice across multiple devices — naming and categorising components repeatedly — builds the precision needed before they can reason about how components combine.

nodes.label: Components working together for a purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explore how components of a digital system work together to serve a specific purpose
criteria: Identifies at least two components used in a specific digital system
Explains how those components work together to achieve the system's purpose

width.minimum: For one familiar digital system, identify the components used and explain how they work together to achieve the system's purpose
width.typical: Explain how components (input, output, processing, storage) work together across different digital systems for different purposes — for example how a camera, screen and storage combine to let you take and keep a photo
wider: Compare how a tablet and a desktop computer achieve the same purpose (e.g. writing a message) using different component combinations — explain why the components differ
Investigate how digital systems provide communities with services — for example how input, processing and output components combine to allow TV to reach remote communities

modes.reason: Component identification and purpose identification are component understandings. At this node students must coordinate both simultaneously — identifying which components are active and explaining how their coordination produces the purpose. This is the integration of the descriptor's two demands: 'identify components' and 'for a purpose'.

descriptors.title: Data as pictures, numbers and words
descriptors.description: represent data as pictures, symbols, numbers and words
descriptors.knowledge: Students can represent data using objects, pictures and symbols (AC9TDIFK02). They have matched physical objects and pictures to what they represent. They have not yet worked with multiple simultaneous representation forms (words, numbers, symbols, pictures) or reasoned about equivalence across forms.
descriptors.endpoint: Students represent the same data using different forms — pictures, symbols, numbers and words — and recognise that different forms can convey equivalent information.

nodes.label: Recognising representation forms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify data represented as pictures, symbols, numbers and words and name which form is being used
criteria: Correctly identifies at least three representation forms from examples
States what information each example conveys
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a recognition repertoire for all four representation forms, Node 2 (representing the same data in multiple forms) lacks the raw material — students cannot produce forms they cannot yet reliably identify.

width.minimum: Given examples of data in different forms, correctly identify each as a picture, symbol, number or word
width.typical: Identify data represented in all four forms across a range of familiar examples (class attendance tally, weather icons, temperature numbers, written labels); explain what information each conveys
wider: Examine First Nations Australians' seasonal calendars where pictures represent connected events and resource availability — identify what data each picture represents and compare to word or number forms of the same information
Explore how the same phoneme can be represented by different letter combinations in written words — connecting data representation to literacy

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of examples of each representation form — a single example of 'a number represents data' is not sufficient to build a reliable category. Repeated encounters across varied contexts (weather, calendar, classroom data) build the recognition repertoire.

nodes.label: Representing the same data in different forms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent the same data using more than one form — for example representing a count as a tally, a number and a word
criteria: Represents one piece of data in at least two distinct forms correctly
Conveys the same information in both forms — the representation is equivalent, not different data
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who still treat different representation forms as containing different information (rather than equivalent information) cannot reason about why forms are chosen in Node 3 — the equivalence understanding must be present before purpose-of-form reasoning can proceed.

width.minimum: Represent one piece of data in at least two different forms (e.g. draw a picture and write a number for the same quantity)
width.typical: Represent the same data (e.g. class pet vote results, weather observation, attendance count) in three or more forms — picture, tally/number, word, and symbol — and explain that the forms show the same information
wider: Create a class data display using different representation forms for the same dataset — for example representing favourite foods as a picture graph, a tally chart and a written sentence
Explore how a tally mark and a digit are both ways to represent numbers — count the same collection using both and compare

modes.reason: Students often treat different representation forms as containing different information rather than equivalent information. Encountering the same data in multiple forms across several contexts (not just one) helps build the equivalence understanding — the data is the same, only the representation changes.

nodes.label: Recognising equivalence across forms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise that different representation forms — pictures, symbols, numbers and words — can convey the same data, and explain why different forms may be used
criteria: Confirms two different representations of the same data are equivalent
Gives at least one reason why each representation form might be useful

width.minimum: Given two different representations of the same data (e.g. a picture and a word), confirm they represent the same thing and suggest one reason why each form might be used
width.typical: Compare several representations of the same dataset; explain that the forms are equivalent and give examples of when each form is most useful (e.g. pictures for quick understanding, numbers for precise counting, words for explaining)
wider: Investigate why First Nations Australians use pictures in seasonal calendars rather than words or numbers — discuss what a picture form conveys that words or numbers might not
Compare how numbers are spelled the same way regardless of accent (spoken form varies, written form is fixed) — connecting representation stability to the purpose of standardised forms

modes.reason: Reasoning about why different forms are used requires students to think about the purpose of representation, not just recognise forms. Scaffolding the reasoning (who is using it? what do they need to know? which form makes that easiest?) prevents students from treating form choice as arbitrary.

descriptors.title: Digital systems and peripherals
descriptors.description: explore and describe a range of digital systems and their peripherals for a variety of purposes
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify and explore digital systems and their components for a purpose (AC9TDI2K01). They can name hardware and software as components of digital systems. They have not yet explored the specific categories of peripherals (input, output, storage) or described how peripherals expand system functionality.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore and describe a range of digital systems and their peripherals, explaining how different peripherals serve input, output and storage purposes and how they expand what a digital system can do.

nodes.label: Peripherals as categories
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sort peripherals into input, output and storage categories and give an example of each
criteria: Correctly places at least two peripherals in each of the three categories
Explains what input, output and storage each mean in plain language
nodes.hinge_reason: Category confusion between input and output (treating the monitor as 'the computer') propagates into N2 and N3 — students who cannot classify peripherals by data-flow direction cannot reason about what adding a peripheral enables or which peripheral suits a purpose.

width.minimum: Name at least one example of an input peripheral, one output peripheral, and one storage peripheral; explain the job each category performs
width.typical: Classify a range of familiar peripherals (keyboard, mouse, microphone, camera; monitor, printer, speaker; USB drive) into input, output and storage categories and explain the function of each
wider: Investigate how peripherals used in First Nations community contexts (e.g. GPS devices used by rangers, shared devices in remote schools) are classified and what purposes they serve
Explore how a touchscreen device combines input and output in a single peripheral — discuss why this blurs the category boundaries

modes.reason: Students commonly conflate input and output or treat the monitor as 'the computer'. More examples across varied peripheral types help students see what defines the category (direction of data flow) rather than memorising a fixed list.

nodes.label: Peripherals expand functionality
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how adding a peripheral changes what a digital system can do
criteria: Names a peripheral and correctly identifies the new capability it adds
Does not confuse the peripheral itself with the system it connects to
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot explain the causal link (peripheral → new capability) cannot make purposeful peripheral selection decisions in N3 — they revert to guessing or listing familiar peripherals.

width.minimum: Describe one example of a peripheral being added to a digital system and explain what new capability it gives the system
width.typical: Explain how different peripherals (headset, camera, printer, USB drive) each add a specific capability to a digital system; identify which peripheral would be needed for a given task
wider: Research how 3D printers as output peripherals have changed what schools and designers can produce — compare 3D printing to standard printing as output devices
Investigate how peripherals for accessibility (e.g. screen readers, switch controllers) expand what a digital system can do for different users

modes.reason: Students need to reason from 'what does this peripheral do?' to 'what can the system now do that it couldn't before?' — a causal reasoning step that benefits from explicit scaffolding rather than assuming students make the connection.

nodes.label: Choosing peripherals for purposes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe which digital system and peripherals are appropriate for a given task and explain why
criteria: Identifies at least one peripheral appropriate for a described task
Gives a reason for the choice that references the peripheral's function

width.minimum: Given a task (e.g. recording a class presentation), identify the digital system and at least one peripheral needed and explain why they suit the task
width.typical: Explain how different tasks require different combinations of digital systems and peripherals; describe how the same digital system (e.g. a tablet) can serve different purposes depending on which peripherals or features are used
wider: Compare how a student in a city school and a student in a remote community might use different digital systems and peripherals to complete the same task — discuss what affects those choices
Explore how digital systems used in scientific data collection (e.g. sensors, cameras in field research) combine specialist peripherals for specific purposes

modes.reason: Students often anchor on a single device type (e.g. 'you need a computer'). Exploring varied task contexts — recording, presenting, communicating, storing — surfaces the idea that purpose drives peripheral selection.
This node integrates the category knowledge from node 1 and the functionality reasoning from node 2 into a purposeful selection decision — the components come together in a task-driven context.

descriptors.title: Transmitting data between systems
descriptors.description: explore transmitting different types of data between digital systems
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify digital systems and represent data as pictures, symbols, numbers and words (AC9TDI2K01, AC9TDI2K02). They have not yet explored how data moves between digital systems or considered the types of data that can be transmitted.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how different types of data (text, audio, video, images) can be transmitted between digital systems, and describe examples of data transmission in everyday contexts.

nodes.label: Data types that can be transmitted
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the different types of data that digital systems can transmit and give an example of each
criteria: Names at least two distinct data types correctly
Matches each type to a concrete real-world transmission example
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot name and categorise data types cannot describe what is being transmitted in N2 — descriptions collapse to 'stuff going between devices' without conceptual grounding.

width.minimum: Name at least two types of data (e.g. text, audio, video, images) that can be sent between digital systems and give one example of each type being transmitted
width.typical: Identify text, audio, video and image as data types that can be transmitted; provide concrete examples of each (e.g. messaging, streaming music, video calls, photo sharing)
wider: Investigate what types of data are transmitted when a First Nations community ranger sends location data via GPS — discuss what data types are involved and how they combine
Explore how sensor data (e.g. temperature, movement) is a type of data that can be transmitted — compare to more familiar types like images and text

nodes.label: How data moves between systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe what happens when data is transmitted between digital systems — that data travels from one system to another across a connection
criteria: Identifies sender and receiver in a described data transmission
Names the type of data being transmitted

width.minimum: Describe one example of data being sent from one digital system to another and identify the sender, data type and receiver
width.typical: Describe several examples of data transmission (streaming music on a smartphone, making a video call, sending a file) identifying what data moves from which system to which; recognise that a network or connection is needed
wider: Explore how video call data can be transmitted from a remote First Nations community to a city location — investigate how 3G network limitations affect the quality and reliability of video data transmission
Investigate how data is transmitted when downloading a game or app — discuss the path data takes between a server and the student's device

modes.reason: Students often think of data transmission only in terms of internet browsing. Exploring diverse examples — video calls, music streaming, file sharing — builds a more generalised understanding of data moving between systems rather than memorising one context.

descriptors.title: Data types and representations
descriptors.description: recognise different types of data and explore how the same data can be represented differently depending on the purpose
descriptors.knowledge: Students can represent data using pictures, symbols, numbers and words (AC9TDI2K02). They have explored data as objects and symbols at Foundation level. They have not yet explored how the same data can be represented in multiple ways or why one representation might suit a purpose better than another.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise different types of data (numbers, text, symbols, images) and explain how the same data can be represented in different ways, giving reasons why particular representations suit particular purposes.

nodes.label: Types of data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and name different types of data — numbers, text, symbols and images — and give examples of each
criteria: Names at least three distinct types of data correctly
Matches each type to at least one concrete example

width.minimum: Name and give one example each of at least three types of data (e.g. numbers, letters, symbols, pictures)
width.typical: Identify numbers, text, symbols and images as distinct data types; describe how each is used in familiar digital and non-digital contexts (e.g. numerals in a calculator, letters in a message, icons on a phone)
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australian rock paintings use images to encode knowledge about plants and animals — discuss how images are a data type that carries structured information
Explore emoji as a data type — discuss whether they are symbols, images or a distinct category, and what kinds of meaning they can and cannot convey

nodes.label: Multiple representations of the same data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can give examples of the same data shown in different ways and explain that different representations exist for the same underlying information
criteria: Identifies two different representations of the same data
States that both representations carry the same underlying information
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who only know that representations exist but treat them as equivalent (no better/worse) cannot engage with N3's purpose-fitness reasoning — the N3 question ('why this representation?') is meaningless if students think all representations are interchangeable.

width.minimum: Give one example of the same data represented in two different ways (e.g. the number 4 as '4', 'four', and 'IV') and state that both represent the same value
width.typical: Explain several examples of the same data in different representations (numerals vs words vs tally vs Roman numerals; 'stop' vs stop sign vs hand icon); recognise that representations can use different formats to convey the same information
wider: Compare how the same geographic location data can be represented as coordinates, a street address, a place name and a map pin — investigate which representation suits which purpose

Explore how the Kimberley cave paintings encode ethnobotanical knowledge — compare how the same information about plant use might be represented in a modern classification system vs an image-based system

modes.reason: Students easily understand one representation pair but often think the difference is about correctness rather than purpose-fitness. Multiple examples across different data types (numeric, symbolic, iconic) help students see that representation is a design choice, not a matter of right and wrong.

nodes.label: Why representation depends on purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why some representations suit a purpose better than others, with reference to a specific example
criteria: States a reason why a particular representation suits a given purpose
Does not simply state that one representation is 'better' without reference to the context or audience

width.minimum: Given two representations of the same data, state which is better suited to a given purpose and give one reason
width.typical: Explain why different representations suit different purposes across multiple examples (e.g. numerals better for calculation than words; an icon better for a multilingual audience than a text label); apply this reasoning to a new example
wider: Investigate how data about a person's health or location might be represented differently for a doctor, a researcher and the person themselves — discuss how purpose shapes the representation chosen

Explore how First Nations Australian knowledge systems use image-based representations of plant and animal data — discuss what kinds of knowledge are well-suited to image representation versus text or number

modes.reason: The jump from 'there are different representations' to 'this representation suits this purpose' requires explicit reasoning about the relationship between format and use. Students need a scaffold for reasoning about purpose-fitness, not just example recall.
The 'better for purpose' concept only becomes generalisable when students encounter it across varied data types and audiences. Single-example exposure risks students treating one pair as the rule.

descriptors.title: Internal components and function
descriptors.description: Investigate the main internal components of common digital systems and their function
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore and describe a range of digital systems and their peripherals for a variety of purposes (AC9TDI4K01). They understand that digital systems have input and output components. They have not yet investigated what happens inside a digital system — internal components and their specific functions remain unexplored.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate the main internal components of common digital systems (CPU, memory, input/output components, storage) and explain how each component performs a specific function within the system.

nodes.label: Digital systems are made of parts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that digital systems are made up of distinct internal components, each performing a specific function
criteria: Names at least two internal components of a digital system
States the function of each named component in plain language
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify what each component does cannot reason about how components coordinate in N2 — the 'how they work together' task requires knowing each part's role as a prerequisite.

width.minimum: Name at least two internal components of a digital system and state what each does
width.typical: Identify the main internal components (CPU, RAM, storage, input/output) of a familiar digital system such as a tablet or desktop; describe the function of each component in plain language
wider: Compare internal components across different digital systems — a smartphone versus a gaming console versus a laptop — identifying which components are shared and which differ
Investigate the internal components of a telehealth system used to access ultrasound imagery in remote communities, identifying which components support sending and receiving large image files

modes.reason: Students at this node commonly confuse 'the device' with 'the component' — treating the whole system as a single thing. Seeing the same component (e.g. a CPU) appear in different devices (tablet, console, laptop) with different physical forms but the same function helps students separate the component from any single device form factor.

nodes.label: How CPU, memory and I/O work together
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the CPU, memory and input/output components work together to perform a task
criteria: Correctly assigns at least three roles (input, process, memory, output) to the correct component in a given task
Explains what each component contributes without treating them as interchangeable

width.minimum: Trace through a simple calculation or task (e.g. entering numbers and getting a sum) and identify which component handles each step — input, processing, memory, output
width.typical: Explain how CPU, RAM and input/output components each play a role in completing a simple task; describe what would happen if one component were missing or very slow
wider: Investigate how video conferencing systems combine multiple input/output components (camera, microphone, screen, speaker) and explain how the CPU coordinates them simultaneously
Explore how a calculator app on a tablet uses each component differently from a web browser — which components are used most and why?

modes.reason: Students need to reason about a process rather than just name components. The input → process → memory → output chain is a reasoning scaffold, not just a label set. Explicitly tracing a task step-by-step helps students build this as a thinking pattern rather than a memorised sequence.

This node is where the individual component facts from Node 1 become a system understanding. Coordinating all four components in a single task trace is the learning — not any one component in isolation.

descriptors.title: Networks and data transmission
descriptors.description: Examine how digital systems form networks to transmit data
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore the transmission of different types of data between digital systems (AC9TDI4K02). They understand that data can move between devices. They have not yet examined how networks are structured, how devices connect to form them, or how data is structured for transmission (packets).
descriptors.endpoint: Students examine how digital systems connect in different ways to form networks, and explain how data is structured and transmitted through a network from source to destination.

nodes.label: How separate systems connect to form networks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how separate digital systems can be connected in different ways to exchange data
criteria: Names at least two ways a device can connect to a network
Explains that connecting devices allows data to be exchanged between them
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have not grasped that separate devices connect to form networks cannot follow the packet transmission model in N2 — the path a packet travels requires understanding there is a network of connected devices for it to traverse.

width.minimum: Describe at least two ways a device can connect to a network (e.g. cable, Wi-Fi) and explain that connecting devices allows them to exchange data
width.typical: Explain how a laptop or device can connect to a network via a physical cable or radio waves (Wi-Fi/Bluetooth); compare when each type of connection is more appropriate
wider: Investigate how satellite phones provide network access where mobile phone networks are unavailable, such as in remote Arnhem Land communities — explaining why different network infrastructure is needed in these locations
Compare how the same device (e.g. a laptop) uses different connection types in different situations — wired at school, Wi-Fi at home, mobile data travelling — and why the network experience differs

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse the connection type (cable vs wireless) with the network itself — thinking the wire is the internet rather than a path to it. Multiple connection contexts (home, school, remote area) help students see that the network is the shared infrastructure, not the physical medium.

nodes.label: How data travels through a network
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how data is structured into packets and transmitted through multiple devices from source to destination
criteria: Explains that data is broken into packets for network transmission
Describes that packets travel through multiple devices to reach the destination

width.minimum: Explain that data is broken into packets for transmission and these packets travel from the source through multiple devices to the destination
width.typical: Describe how data is broken into packets, transmitted through multiple intermediate devices, and reassembled at the destination; explain why breaking data into packets is useful (e.g. packets can take different routes, errors affect only one packet)
wider: Investigate what happens when a packet is lost or delayed — how does the destination device detect missing data and request retransmission?
Compare how packet size and number of intermediate devices (hops) affects transmission speed and reliability in different network types

modes.reason: The packet model is counter-intuitive — students expect data to travel as a single stream like water through a pipe. Tracing a message as packets through a diagrammed network (source → router → router → destination) makes the multi-step transmission legible and challenges the 'direct connection' mental model.

descriptors.title: Data represented as numbers
descriptors.description: Explain how digital systems represent all data using numbers
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise different types of data and explore how the same data can be represented differently depending on context (AC9TDI4K03). They understand that data exists in different forms (text, images, numbers). They have not yet connected the idea that digital systems ultimately represent all these different data types as numbers.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how digital systems represent all types of data — text, images, sound — as numbers, and understand that the data type determines what operations can be performed.

nodes.label: Text as numbers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how text characters are represented as numbers in a digital system
criteria: Explains that text characters are stored as numbers in a digital system
Can demonstrate a simple letter-to-number conversion
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have not grasped that data is represented as numbers cannot engage with N2's data type reasoning — if a student does not accept that 'A' and 65 are the same stored value in different interpretations, the concept that type determines operations has no foundation.

width.minimum: Convert letters in a short message to numbers using a positional scheme (e.g. A=1, B=2) and explain that digital systems use similar numeric encoding for text
width.typical: Explain that each character in a digital system is assigned a number (like ASCII or Unicode); demonstrate with examples how text characters — letters, numbers, symbols — each map to a unique number that the system stores and processes
wider: Investigate how Unicode allows characters from non-English scripts (e.g. Chinese, Arabic, First Nations language characters) to be encoded numerically — why a single scheme matters for global communication
Explore how emoji are also assigned numeric codes — explaining that an emoji is stored as a number just like the letter 'A' is

modes.reason: Students readily accept that the number '5' is stored as a number, but resist the idea that the letter 'A' is also stored as a number — it seems like a category error. Multiple encoding contexts (letters, emoji, non-Latin scripts) help students generalise: all characters, regardless of type, are ultimately numbers.

nodes.label: Data type determines what you can do
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the data type used to represent data changes what operations can be performed on it
criteria: Gives a correct example where the same value behaves differently based on data type
Explains in plain language why data type affects what operations are possible

width.minimum: Give one example showing that the same value behaves differently depending on its data type — e.g. adding '3' + '4' gives 7 when they are numbers but '34' when they are strings
width.typical: Explain that numbers support arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction) while text supports string operations (joining, searching); demonstrate both with examples; explain why digital systems need to know which type they are working with
wider: Investigate how treating a phone number as a number versus a string causes real problems — adding phone numbers is meaningless, but searching within them (e.g. all numbers starting with 04) requires string operations
Explore how images are also represented as numbers (each pixel has a numeric colour value) and what kinds of operations this enables — adjusting brightness by changing pixel values mathematically

modes.reason: Students often treat data types as arbitrary naming conventions rather than a meaningful distinction. Concrete cases where the type matters (phone number as number vs string, pixel values as arithmetic) help students see that the type determines what operations make sense — not just what the value looks like.

The reasoning pattern here (identify data → identify operation → check if type supports operation → predict outcome) is the key skill. Scaffolding this as an explicit reasoning chain prevents students from guessing rather than reasoning.

descriptors.title: Binary representation
descriptors.description: Explore how data can be represented by off and on states (zeros and ones in binary)
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how digital systems represent all data using numbers (AC9TDI6K03). They understand that text and other data types are stored as numbers. They have not yet explored how numbers themselves are represented in a digital system — the binary (on/off) basis of all digital data.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how on/off states in digital circuits can represent zeros and ones, and how binary is the fundamental representation underlying all digital data.

nodes.label: On/off states represent zero and one
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that an on/off state in a digital circuit represents the digits one and zero
criteria: Explains that an on/off state represents 1 and 0 in a digital system
Gives at least one example of a two-state system representing binary data
nodes.hinge_reason: The on/off state = 0/1 concept is definitionally required for N2 — without it, the integration of numeric representation (K03) with physical storage cannot proceed. N2's chain (data → number → binary → physical state) collapses at the last step.

width.minimum: Demonstrate or explain that a two-state system (on/off, yes/no, long/short) can represent 1 and 0; connect this to how digital systems store data at the physical level
width.typical: Demonstrate that an on/off state in a circuit represents 1 and 0; recognise that yes/no questions, Morse code dashes and dots, and circuit states all use the same two-state principle; explain that digital systems use billions of these switches to store complex data
wider: Create a binary representation of a word or phrase (e.g. the name of a local Country/Place in a First Nations language) using beads, switches or symbols — demonstrating that any two-state medium can encode binary data
Investigate how punch cards or early telegraph systems used physical two-state mechanisms to encode information before electronic computers existed

modes.reason: Students often struggle to see that binary is an abstract principle, not a specific technology. Seeing the same on/off structure in circuits, Morse code, beads, and yes/no questions helps students abstract the principle: any two distinguishable states can encode 0 and 1.

nodes.label: Binary connects numeric representation to physical storage
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how binary connects the numeric representation of data (from AC9TDI6K03) to the physical on/off states in a digital system
criteria: Connects the idea that data is stored as numbers to the idea that numbers are stored as binary sequences
Can describe the on/off state interpretation of at least one binary digit

width.minimum: Explain that numbers stored in a digital system are ultimately represented as sequences of on/off states — each digit (0 or 1) corresponds to one switch state
width.typical: Trace the connection from data (e.g. the letter 'A') → number (65 in ASCII) → binary sequence (01000001) → physical on/off states; explain each step in the chain
wider: Represent a short word in binary using a provided encoding table; explain that the digital system performs this translation billions of times per second
Investigate how the number of binary digits (bits) limits how many different values can be stored — 1 bit = 2 values, 2 bits = 4 values, 8 bits = 256 values

modes.reason: This node integrates the data-as-numbers understanding from K03 with the binary/on-off understanding from K04 node 1. Tracing the full chain (data → number → binary → physical state) is the integration act — students who cannot connect these steps have two disconnected facts rather than a system understanding.

descriptors.title: Hardware specifications and performance
descriptors.description: Explain how hardware specifications affect performance and select appropriate hardware for particular tasks and workloads
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify and explain the main internal components of common digital systems and their functions (AC9TDI6K01). They understand that digital systems form networks to transmit data (AC9TDI6K02). They have not yet connected hardware specifications to performance outcomes or made selection decisions based on workload requirements.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how specific hardware specifications (RAM, bandwidth, storage, GPU/CPU) affect the speed and capability of digital systems, and select appropriate hardware for particular tasks by matching specifications to workload requirements.

nodes.label: What hardware specifications are
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify key hardware specifications (RAM, storage, bandwidth, processor type) and explain what each measures
criteria: Names at least three hardware specifications correctly
Explains what each specification measures in plain language
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify and name hardware specifications correctly cannot reason about how those specifications affect performance at Node 2. Vague or confused specification vocabulary (e.g. conflating storage with RAM) propagates through every subsequent reasoning task about workloads.

width.minimum: Name at least three hardware specifications and state what each measures in a digital system
width.typical: Identify specifications across different device types (phone, laptop, server); explain why the same specification (e.g. RAM) matters differently in each context
wider: Research the specifications of devices used in remote First Nations communities and explain how shared access affects which specifications matter most
Limited width — comparing marketing claims to benchmark performance goes further analytically rather than exploring specifications across more contexts.

modes.reason: Students who conflate hardware specifications (e.g. treating RAM and storage as equivalent) cannot reason about how different specifications affect performance differently. Seeing the same specification (RAM) behave differently across device contexts (phone vs server) builds the vocabulary precision needed at Node 2.

nodes.label: How specifications affect performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how specific hardware specifications affect what a digital system can do and how quickly it performs
criteria: Explains the causal link between at least one specification and a specific performance outcome
Does not confuse specifications (e.g. storage capacity with processing speed)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot explain the causal link between a specification and a performance outcome cannot make principled hardware selection decisions at Node 3. Without this understanding, Node 3 becomes pattern-matching rather than reasoning.

width.minimum: Explain how one specification (e.g. RAM or bandwidth) affects performance for a given task
width.typical: Explain how different specifications (RAM, bandwidth, storage speed, processor) each affect performance for different tasks; identify which specification is the bottleneck in a given scenario
wider: Explain how GPU specifications affect AI model training speed compared to CPU — why GPUs are more efficient for the mathematical calculations involved
Investigate how bandwidth limitations affect download speed and lag in online gaming or video conferencing

modes.reason: Students who cannot explain the causal link between specifications and performance will guess rather than reason when selecting hardware. Broader contexts (different specs affecting different tasks — gaming, video editing, AI training) help students see the pattern rather than memorise individual spec-task pairs.

nodes.label: Selecting hardware for tasks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select appropriate hardware for a particular task or workload and justify the selection based on specifications
criteria: Selects hardware that matches the task requirements
Justifies the selection by referencing at least one relevant specification

width.minimum: Given a task and two hardware options, select the more appropriate option and justify using at least one specification
width.typical: Compare multiple hardware options for a given workload; justify selection by weighing trade-offs between specifications (e.g. more RAM vs faster processor for video editing)
wider: Research how cloud computing changes hardware selection decisions — when is local hardware insufficient and cloud resources necessary?
Evaluate hardware selection for a real scenario such as setting up a school media lab or an AI training environment

modes.reason: Hardware selection requires students to reason through trade-offs rather than recall a correct answer. Scaffolding the reasoning process (identify task demands → match to specifications → weigh trade-offs → justify) prevents students from pattern-matching rather than reasoning.

descriptors.title: Wired and wireless networks
descriptors.description: Investigate how data is transmitted and secured in wired and wireless networks including the internet
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how digital systems form networks to transmit data (AC9TDI6K02). They have not yet compared wired and wireless network properties, explored encryption, or investigated how protocols handle transmission errors.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how data is transmitted across wired and wireless networks including the internet, by comparing network properties (bandwidth, latency, reliability), explaining how protocols handle packet transmission and errors, and explaining why and how encryption secures data in transit.

nodes.label: Wired vs wireless network properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the properties of wired and wireless networks and compare their bandwidth, latency and reliability
criteria: Correctly names at least two properties that differ between wired and wireless networks
Explains which network type is more suitable for a given use case and why
nodes.hinge_reason: Network properties (bandwidth, latency, reliability) are the vocabulary for Nodes 2–5. Students who cannot name and distinguish these properties cannot reason about why packet loss matters (Node 2), why encryption adds latency (Node 3), or how internet segments work (Node 5).

width.minimum: Name at least two properties that differ between wired and wireless networks; state which is faster or more reliable in a given scenario
width.typical: Compare bandwidth, latency and reliability across wired and wireless networks; explain why each property matters for different uses (e.g. streaming vs file transfer vs gaming)
wider: Research how network infrastructure decisions affect connectivity equity in different communities — why some areas have fibre and others rely on satellite or mobile
Investigate how emerging wireless standards (e.g. Wi-Fi 6, 5G) are narrowing the gap with wired networks

modes.reason: Comparing bandwidth, latency and reliability across use cases (streaming, gaming, file transfer, remote access) builds the conceptual vocabulary needed for Nodes 2 and 5. Students who encounter only one network type cannot generalise the properties when analysing the full internet data journey.

nodes.label: Packets and protocols
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how data is broken into packets for transmission and how protocols like TCP handle errors when packets are lost
criteria: Explains that data is transmitted in packets, not as a continuous stream
Describes what happens when a packet is lost or delayed
nodes.hinge_reason: The packet/protocol model is the prerequisite for understanding why encryption is necessary (Node 3) — students must understand that packets travel through shared infrastructure they don't control before the need for encryption makes sense. Without it, Node 3's reasoning chain fails.

width.minimum: Explain that data is broken into packets for transmission; identify that packets can be lost or delayed in transit
width.typical: Explain how TCP uses acknowledgements to confirm packets have been received; describe what happens when a router drops a packet and how the protocol recovers
wider: Investigate how network problems propagate through systems — what a user experiences when packet loss occurs at different points in the network
Limited width — tracing a full request path from device to server extends the concept further rather than applying packet transmission to a broader range of contexts.

modes.reason: Understanding packet-based transmission is the foundation for both why encryption matters and why protocols exist. Broader contexts (different failure scenarios, different network paths) help students see that packet loss is systemic, not a one-off glitch.

nodes.label: Why data needs to be secured
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why cryptography is necessary for securing data transmitted across networks, connecting the need to how packets travel through shared infrastructure
criteria: Explains why data needs encryption during transmission, not just storage
Names at least one real scenario where encryption protects users
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who accept 'encryption is good' without understanding the shared-infrastructure reasoning cannot explain how simple encryption works (Node 4) or trace the full internet data journey (Node 5). The need for encryption must be understood before the mechanism has meaning.

width.minimum: Explain why data transmitted over a network needs to be encrypted; give one example of data that must be secured (e.g. credit card details, passwords)
width.typical: Explain why encryption is necessary using the shared-infrastructure model — packets pass through routers and systems the sender does not control, so anyone along the path could read unencrypted data
wider: Research why different levels of encryption are used for different types of data — why HTTPS matters for banking but not for reading a public news article
Investigate real cases where unencrypted data transmission led to security breaches — what was exposed and how

modes.reason: The need for encryption is not obvious to students until they reason through the shared-infrastructure model. Scaffolding the chain (packets leave your device → travel through routers you don't control → anyone along the path can read them → therefore encryption is necessary) prevents students from accepting 'encryption is good' as a fact without understanding why.

nodes.label: How simple encryption works
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how simple encryption algorithms transform data to protect it, and demonstrate an encrypt-decrypt cycle
criteria: Describes how a simple algorithm transforms text into an encrypted form
Demonstrates that encryption is reversible — the original message can be recovered

width.minimum: Describe how a simple encryption algorithm (e.g. ROT13) transforms readable text into encrypted text; show that the process is reversible
width.typical: Demonstrate how ROT13 and XOR each encrypt and decrypt a short message; explain why XOR is more useful for digital systems because it operates on binary data
wider: Apply XOR encryption to a short binary message and decrypt it — connect to K04's binary representation

Limited width — encryption algorithms at this level are mechanical demonstrations. Understanding additional algorithms goes further technically rather than broadening the concept of how encryption protects data.

modes.reason: Encryption algorithms at this level are mechanical demonstrations. The encrypt-decrypt cycle needs to be practised until the reversibility principle is automatic — students must be able to demonstrate it fluently before they can reason about why reversibility matters for secure communication.

nodes.label: How the internet transmits and secures data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the internet combines network infrastructure, packet transmission, protocols and encryption to transmit and secure data end to end
criteria: Describes a data journey across the internet that includes at least packets, a protocol and encryption
Identifies where in the journey wired and wireless networks are used

width.minimum: Describe the journey of a piece of data across the internet — from sender through networks to receiver — identifying where packets, protocols and encryption each play a role
width.typical: Trace a real scenario (e.g. making an online purchase) through the full chain: data is encrypted, broken into packets, transmitted across wired and wireless networks via routers, reassembled using TCP, and decrypted at the destination; identify which network properties affect the experience
wider: Investigate how the internet uses both wired and wireless segments in a single data journey — where does fibre end and wireless begin for a typical request?
Research how internet infrastructure differs between urban and remote communities and how this affects the transmission and security chain

modes.reason: This node synthesises all four preceding concepts — network properties, packet transmission, protocols, and encryption — into a single coherent account of how the internet works. Students who have understood each component separately often struggle to assemble them into an end-to-end chain. The integration task surfaces whether components were genuinely understood or merely memorised in isolation.

descriptors.title: Representing text, image and audio
descriptors.description: Investigate how digital systems represent text, image and audio data using integers
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how digital systems use numbers to represent all types of data (AC9TDI6K03) and how data is represented using binary through off and on states (AC9TDI6K04). They understand the general principle that all data is numbers, but have not yet investigated the specific encoding schemes for text, image, or audio.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how digital systems use integers to represent text (Unicode character values), images (RGB pixel values for bitmaps, geometry for SVG), and audio (amplitude samples at a given sampling rate and bit depth), and explain the encoding scheme for each data type.

nodes.label: The principle: all data as integers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that digital systems represent all data types — text, images, audio — as integers, and that different encoding schemes map integers to different kinds of information
criteria: States that all data types are represented as integers in digital systems
Gives at least one example of how a number represents non-numeric information
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand that the same integer means different things in different encoding contexts will treat Nodes 2, 3 and 4 as three unrelated memorisation tasks rather than three instances of the same principle. Without this anchor, the three encoding schemes cannot be integrated at the standard level.

width.minimum: State that text, images and audio are all stored as numbers in a digital system; give one example of how a number could represent non-numeric data
width.typical: Explain that different data types use different encoding schemes — the same integer means different things depending on whether the system is interpreting it as a character, a colour value, or a sound amplitude
wider: Limited width — the encoding-scheme principle does not vary meaningfully across contexts. Reasoning about why a universal scheme would not work goes further conceptually rather than broadening the application of the principle.

modes.reason: If students don't grasp that integers are mapped to meaning through encoding schemes, the three data types (text, images, audio) appear as disconnected facts. Seeing the principle applied across all three types IS the width that resolves the misconception.

nodes.label: Text as Unicode integers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how digital systems represent text as a sequence of characters, each mapped to an integer using the Unicode character set
criteria: Correctly looks up Unicode values for given characters
Explains that each character has a unique integer in the Unicode set
Encodes at least a short word as a sequence of integers

width.minimum: Use a Unicode table to find the integer value for given characters; explain that each character (letter, punctuation, emoji) has a unique number
width.typical: Encode a short word as a sequence of Unicode integers; explain why uppercase and lowercase letters have different values; identify that emoji are also Unicode characters
wider: Investigate how Unicode handles diverse languages and writing systems — why ASCII was insufficient and what Unicode solved
Research how Unicode versioning adds new characters (e.g. emoji) and what that means for backward compatibility

modes.reason: Applying the Unicode encoding scheme across diverse character types (letters, emoji, punctuation, non-Latin scripts) builds robust understanding of the mapping principle rather than a single memorised example. The language diversity direction also connects data representation to cultural and linguistic equity.

nodes.label: Images as pixel colour values
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how digital systems represent bitmap images as RGB colour values per pixel, and how vector graphics use geometry instead
criteria: Explains that bitmap images store RGB values (0-255) for each pixel
Identifies the colour represented by a given RGB triplet
Describes at least one difference between bitmap and vector image representation

width.minimum: Explain that a bitmap image is a grid of pixels, each with RGB colour values from 0 to 255; identify the colour for a given RGB value
width.typical: Calculate the number of integers needed to store a small image given its resolution and colour depth; compare bitmap (PNG/JPEG) and vector (SVG) representations for the same image
wider: Explore how SVG's geometry-based representation enables scaling without quality loss — why this matters for responsive design
Limited width — investigating colour depth trade-offs (8-bit vs 24-bit) goes further technically rather than exploring image representation in a broader range of contexts.

nodes.label: Audio as sampled amplitudes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how digital systems represent audio by sampling the amplitude of a sound wave at regular intervals and storing each sample as an integer
criteria: Explains that audio is represented by sampling amplitude at regular intervals
States that each measurement is stored as an integer

width.minimum: Explain that audio is captured by measuring sound amplitude at regular time intervals; identify that each measurement is stored as an integer
width.typical: Explain how sampling rate (e.g. 44,100 Hz) and bit depth (e.g. 16-bit) determine audio quality; calculate the range of values for a given bit depth
wider: Use a culturally meaningful context such as recording a Welcome to Country to trace how audio data is captured, converted to integers, stored and played back
Limited width — investigating sampling rate and bit depth trade-offs goes further technically rather than applying audio representation to more contexts.

modes.reason: This node connects audio representation to both the principle node (Node 1 — all data as integers) and to K04 (binary representation of those integers). The Welcome to Country context integrates the encoding chain into a culturally meaningful whole.

descriptors.title: Integer representation in binary
descriptors.description: Explain how and why digital systems represent integers in binary
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how data is represented using binary through off and on states (AC9TDI6K04) and how digital systems use integers to represent text, image and audio data (AC9TDI8K03). They understand the concept of binary as on/off, but have not yet explained binary place value, the relationship between bits and representable range, or how circuits perform binary operations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how integers are represented in binary using place value (powers of 2), the relationship between bits, bytes and representable range, and why digital systems use binary — connecting electronic on/off states to logic gates and data encoding.

nodes.label: Binary place value and counting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can count in binary, convert between binary and decimal, and explain binary place value as powers of 2
criteria: Correctly converts at least three decimal numbers to binary
Correctly converts at least three binary numbers to decimal
Explains that each position in a binary number represents a power of 2
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot fluently convert between binary and decimal cannot reason about representable ranges (Node 2), understand how logic gates combine binary states (Node 3), or trace the K03 encoding chain through to binary (Node 4). Conversion errors propagate through all subsequent nodes.

width.minimum: Count in binary from 0 to at least 15; convert a given decimal number to binary and back
width.typical: Convert numbers in both directions confidently; explain that each binary digit represents a power of 2; predict what range of values a given number of bits can represent
wider: Limited width — binary conversion is a mechanical skill that does not vary meaningfully across contexts. Extensions such as binary addition go further conceptually rather than broadening the application of place value.

modes.reason: Binary conversion is a mechanical skill that all subsequent understanding depends on. Width is thin — there are no meaningfully different contexts for conversion. What helps is more practice: more conversions, more checking, building fluency until conversion is automatic.

nodes.label: Bits, bytes and range
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the relationship between the number of bits and the range of values that can be represented, and use standard units (byte = 8 bits)
criteria: States that 1 byte = 8 bits and can represent values from 0 to 255
Does not confuse bit count with the values themselves (e.g. 8 bits does not mean the number 8)

width.minimum: State that 1 byte = 8 bits and can represent values from 0 to 255
width.typical: Explain why 8 bits gives 256 possible values (2^8); predict the range for different bit counts; connect byte size to practical examples from K03 (e.g. RGB values 0-255 are one byte per channel, 16-bit audio uses 2 bytes per sample)
wider: Calculate the storage requirements for a small image or short audio clip using bit depth and resolution, connecting bits/bytes to real data representation from K03
Limited width — overflow errors go further conceptually rather than applying the bits-to-range relationship across more contexts.

modes.reason: This node connects binary representation (K04) back to data encoding (K03) — the bits/bytes/range relationship grounds the earlier encoding discussion in concrete number theory. Students who only memorise '1 byte = 8 bits' without connecting it to K03 RGB/audio examples have not integrated the two standards.

nodes.label: Why binary — circuits and logic gates
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why digital systems use binary by connecting electronic on/off states to how circuits perform operations using logic gates
criteria: Explains that binary maps to the two reliable states of electronic components
Demonstrates the output of AND and OR gates for given inputs
Connects logic gates to why digital systems are built on binary

width.minimum: Explain that computers use binary because electronic components have two reliable states (on/off); identify that circuits with switches can represent AND or OR operations
width.typical: Demonstrate how a 2-switch circuit represents AND and OR gates; explain the output for each combination of inputs; connect this to why binary is the foundation for all computation
wider: Limited width — logic gates and circuit-level operations do not vary meaningfully across contexts. Extensions such as adder circuits or the history of binary vs analogue computing go further conceptually rather than broadening the application.

modes.reason: The why-binary question requires students to reason through a chain: electronic components have two reliable states → those states can be encoded as 0/1 → circuits can combine those states using Boolean logic → therefore binary is the natural foundation. Students who skip this reasoning and accept 'computers use binary' as a given cannot explain why binary was chosen over other number bases.

nodes.label: Binary connects to data encoding
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how binary integer representation underpins the encoding of text, images and audio, connecting K04 to K03
criteria: Traces a character from text to Unicode value to binary representation
Explains that all data types ultimately become sequences of binary digits
Connects the encoding chain from K03 (data as integers) to K04 (integers as binary)

width.minimum: Trace one example from data to binary: convert a character to its Unicode integer, then convert that integer to binary
width.typical: Trace the full encoding chain for two data types (e.g. a character via Unicode to binary, and a pixel colour via RGB to binary); explain why binary is the final representation for all data types
wider: Limited width — the integration of binary with data encoding is the endpoint of this standard. Extensions such as file formats or compression go beyond the standard's scope into Year 9-10 territory.

modes.reason: This node is the explicit cross-standard integration point between K03 and K04. Students must assemble the full encoding chain — data type → integer → binary — to demonstrate that both standards are genuinely understood and not held as separate compartments.

descriptors.title: Managing and securing networked systems
descriptors.description: investigate how hardware and software manage, control and secure access to data in networked digital systems
descriptors.knowledge: Students can investigate how data is transmitted and secured in wired and wireless networks, including the use of protocols (AC9TDI8K02). They can explain how hardware specifications affect performance (AC9TDI8K01). They have not yet examined the software layer (OS, access control, cryptography) that manages and secures data in networked systems.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how hardware and software components — including operating systems, access control mechanisms, and cryptographic protocols — work together to manage, control and secure access to data in networked digital systems.

nodes.label: The OS as a hardware abstraction layer
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the operating system hides the complexity of different hardware from applications, allowing software to treat different hardware uniformly.
criteria: Correctly describes the OS as sitting between hardware and applications
Uses a specific example to illustrate how abstraction works (e.g. mouse and touchscreen treated the same by an application)

width.minimum: Explain, using one example, how the OS allows applications to interact with hardware without knowing the hardware's specifics.
width.typical: Explain how the OS abstracts different input devices, storage types, and network interfaces; describe the role of device drivers in this abstraction.
wider: Compare how the same application behaves across different operating systems and explain what the OS must do to make this possible
Investigate how OS-level hardware abstraction affects accessibility features — for example, how the OS allows screen readers to work across multiple input types

nodes.label: Network addressing and routing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how domain names and IP addresses allow data to be transmitted to specific devices on a network.
criteria: Correctly distinguishes IP addresses from domain names
Explains the role of DNS in translating between the two
Describes how routing tables direct packets toward their destination
nodes.hinge_reason: Confusion between IP addresses and domain names, or misunderstanding of how packets are routed, propagates into N4 and N5 — students cannot reason about where cryptographic protection applies or trace a complete data flow without correctly understanding how addressing and routing work.

width.minimum: Explain the role of IP addresses in identifying devices on a network and describe how DNS translates domain names to IP addresses.
width.typical: Explain how IP addresses, DNS and routing tables work together to direct data packets to the correct destination across a network; describe the difference between public and private IP addresses.
wider: Trace a DNS lookup and packet routing path for a request to a website, identifying each step from browser to server
Investigate how the transition from IPv4 to IPv6 addresses the limitation of available addresses and what this means for networked device growth

modes.reason: Students frequently conflate IP addresses with domain names, or assume routing is a single hop. Multiple tracing activities — DNS lookup, packet path, address types — resolve these conflations more effectively than repeating the same explanation.

nodes.label: Access control mechanisms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe elements of access control — including authentication and permissions — and explain why they are necessary in networked systems.
criteria: Distinguishes authentication from authorisation/permissions correctly
Explains what a specific access control mechanism protects against in a networked context
nodes.hinge_reason: Conflation of authentication and authorisation cascades into N5 — students who cannot distinguish 'proving identity' from 'granting access rights' cannot analyse how a networked system's security components coordinate.

width.minimum: Describe at least one access control mechanism (e.g. passwords/authentication OR file permissions) and explain what it protects against.
width.typical: Explain the difference between authentication (proving identity) and permissions/authorisation (what an authenticated user may do); describe how each operates in a networked system with multiple users.
wider: Investigate how role-based access control (RBAC) is implemented in enterprise systems and why it is more scalable than individual permission assignment
Examine how misconfigured permissions have caused real data breaches — what access control failure occurred and what should have been in place

modes.reason: Students often conflate authentication and authorisation. A reasoning scaffold — who are you? (authentication) → what are you allowed to do? (authorisation) → what should the system block? (enforcement) — helps students distinguish these systematically rather than mixing up the terms.

nodes.label: Cryptographic security mechanisms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how public key cryptography and hashing are used to secure the transmission and storage of data in networked systems.
criteria: Correctly explains what public key cryptography protects (data in transit) and how it does so
Correctly explains what hashing protects (stored data / integrity verification) and how it differs from encryption
nodes.hinge_reason: Conflating encryption with hashing, or treating all cryptography as identical, breaks the N5 integration — students cannot correctly identify which mechanism protects data in transit versus at rest.

width.minimum: Explain, in plain language, how one cryptographic mechanism (e.g. TLS for transmission OR hashing for storage) protects data.
width.typical: Explain how public key cryptography (e.g. TLS) secures data in transit and how hashing (e.g. SHA-1) protects stored data; describe the different threat each addresses.
wider: Investigate how certificate authorities establish trust in public key cryptography — what happens when a certificate is invalid or expired?
Explore how modern systems combine symmetric and asymmetric encryption to gain the security benefits of asymmetric without the performance cost
Research how First Nations community health data is protected using encryption standards in remote health systems — why data sovereignty requirements shape cryptographic choices

modes.reason: Cryptography is conceptually dense — students often conflate encryption with hashing, or assume all encryption is the same. Multiple concrete examples (HTTPS padlock, password storage, certificate chain) each illuminate a different aspect and build the distinction through contrast.

nodes.label: Integration — how hardware and software work together in secured networks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate a networked digital system and explain how its hardware and software components — addressing, access control, and cryptography — work together to manage and secure data.
criteria: Identifies the role of at least two distinct components in securing data in a networked system
Explains how the components interact — not just what each does individually

width.minimum: Describe how at least two components (e.g. OS + authentication, OR routing + TLS) work together to secure data in a networked system.
width.typical: Trace data through a networked system — from a user request, through DNS/routing, authenticated access, to encrypted transmission — and identify where each security mechanism operates.
wider: Configure a simple simulated network and observe packets moving between devices — identify what is encrypted, what is routed, and what access controls are applied at each stage
Analyse a real or simulated network breach to identify which layers of the system failed and what should have prevented it

modes.reason: Nodes 1–4 address hardware abstraction, addressing, access control, and cryptography as separate components. The integration node is where students must coordinate all four — understanding that securing a networked system requires all mechanisms to work together. Phase failure here is describing each mechanism correctly but unable to explain how they interact.

descriptors.title: Content, structure and presentation separation
descriptors.description: represent documents online as content (text), structure (markup) and presentation (styling) and explain why such representations are important
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use a range of digital tools to create and communicate content (AC9TDI8P11, AC9TDI8P12). They have not yet formally encountered the three-layer model of web documents or the rationale for separating content, structure and presentation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students represent online documents by separating content (text), structure (HTML markup) and presentation (CSS styling), and explain why this separation is important for design, maintenance and accessibility.

nodes.label: The three layers of a web document
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and distinguish the three layers of an online document: content, structure and presentation.
criteria: Correctly assigns specific examples (e.g. heading text, <h1> tag, font-size rule) to the correct layer
Does not confuse structural tags with visual appearance
nodes.hinge_reason: Misidentifying what belongs to content, structure, or presentation directly prevents N2 — students who conflate layers cannot correctly use HTML for structure and CSS for presentation.

width.minimum: Given a web page, identify what is content (text), what is structure (markup that organises the document), and what is presentation (how it looks).
width.typical: Describe what each layer contains and what role it plays; identify examples of HTML structural tags and CSS presentation rules in a web page.
wider: Compare how the same HTML document renders with and without CSS — articulate specifically what changed and what did not
Investigate how a screen reader interprets an HTML document and explain how structure (not presentation) determines what is communicated to the user

modes.reason: Distinguishing three layers is a precision task — students commonly assign CSS rules to 'structure' or treat HTML tags as presentation. Sufficient practice mapping specific examples (this text, this tag, this rule) to the correct layer builds the reliable discrimination needed before N2.

nodes.label: Representing documents with HTML and CSS
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write web pages using HTML for content and structure and CSS for styling, and explain how HTML tags separate content from structure.
criteria: HTML file uses structural tags correctly (headings, paragraphs, at minimum)
CSS rule targets an HTML element or class and changes its presentation
Student can explain what the HTML tag does versus what the CSS rule does
nodes.hinge_reason: Syntactic fluency at N2 is prerequisite for N3 — students who cannot produce working HTML/CSS cannot demonstrate the separation principle in action; they can only describe it abstractly, which does not meet the descriptor's demand.

width.minimum: Write a simple web page with at least two structural HTML elements and one CSS rule applied to them; explain what the tag does versus what the CSS rule does.
width.typical: Create a web page using HTML structural tags (headings, paragraphs, lists, divs) and CSS rules (colour, font, layout); explain how changing the CSS changes presentation without altering structure.
wider: Apply CSS classes to demonstrate how the same structural element can have different presentations in different contexts on the same page
Use CSS to implement a responsive layout that changes presentation based on screen width, explaining how presentation changes while structure remains constant

modes.reason: HTML/CSS syntax requires precision — misplaced tags, missing closing elements, and selector errors are common. Students need sufficient practice with the syntax to develop fluency before the conceptual significance of separation is legible to them.

nodes.label: Why separation matters
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why separating content, structure and presentation is important — specifically how it allows each to be designed, edited and stored independently.
criteria: Explains at least one concrete benefit of separation with a specific example
Connects the benefit to a real consequence (e.g. changing one CSS file updates many pages)

width.minimum: Give at least one reason why separating content, structure and presentation is important — with a concrete example of the benefit.
width.typical: Explain multiple benefits of separation: independent editing, consistent presentation across many pages via a single CSS file, accessibility (structure legible to screen readers), and easier maintenance.
wider: Demonstrate the maintenance benefit by changing one CSS file to restyle an entire multi-page site, explaining why this would be impractical if styling were embedded in content
Investigate how major content management systems (e.g. WordPress themes) implement content/structure/presentation separation and explain the architectural choices
Examine how First Nations language preservation websites use structured content to support multiple language versions of the same page — explaining why structure separation makes this feasible

modes.reason: Students who have only produced a single small web page often struggle to appreciate why separation matters — the benefit is invisible at small scale. Multiple contexts (site-wide restyling, screen reader accessibility, multi-language content) each illuminate a different reason, making the principle concrete across scales.

descriptors.title: Data compression techniques
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how digital systems represent text, image and audio data using binary (AC9TDI8K03) and how integers are represented in binary (AC9TDI8K04). They understand that different data types require different amounts of storage. They have not yet investigated how data can be compressed to reduce storage and transmission requirements.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate simple data compression techniques, including lossless methods such as run-length encoding and lossy methods, and explain the difference between lossy and lossless compression and the consequences of each.

nodes.label: Why compression is needed
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why data compression is useful and identify contexts where it matters.
